coachMessages.text: Red always goes first. In any empty column, who lands on the bottom cell? Who lands one above? Follow the sequence.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show a single empty column (e.g., col 3). Use alternating overlays to mark the first three cells from the bottom with player labels: row 0 marked 'tg' with label 'Red (move 1)', row 1 marked 'td' with label 'Yellow (move 2)', row 2 marked 'tg' with label 'Red (move 3)'. All other columns empty. Legend: 'tg' = Red's cell, 'td' = Yellow's cell.</board instructions>

Red plays first, so the first disc in any empty column always belongs to Red — that is row 0 (0-indexed, bottom). Yellow lands at row 1, Red at row 2, Yellow at row 3, and so on. The pattern never breaks.

Two equivalent ways to say this:
- **0-indexed:** Red owns rows 0, 2, 4 (even numbers)
- **1-indexed (as used in most books):** Red owns rows 1, 3, 5 (odd numbers)

Both say the same thing. This lesson uses 0-indexed coordinates throughout.

coachMessages.text: Each column runs its own alternation independently. Count the discs already in the column — that tells you who owns the next cell.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show a mid-game board where three columns have different heights: one column is empty (0 discs), one has 1 disc (Red at bottom), one has 2 discs (Red then Yellow). For each column, mark the next available empty cell with a player-coloured overlay: empty column → 'tg' (Red goes next), 1-disc column → 'td' (Yellow goes next), 2-disc column → 'tg' (Red goes next). Legend: 'tg' = Red's next cell in this column, 'td' = Yellow's next cell in this column.</board instructions>

Each column has its own mini-game. Count how many discs are already there — the next disc in that column belongs to whoever is next in the alternation for that column's current height. The global rule (Red first everywhere) means: if a column has an even number of discs (0, 2, 4…), the next disc is Red's; if it has an odd number (1, 3, 5…), the next disc is Yellow's.

coachMessages.text: Watch out: the same row number can belong to different players in different columns. The row alone doesn't tell you who owns it.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show a board with two columns that both have an empty cell at row 2, but one column has 0 discs already (so row 2 is Red's — 2 empty cells below it) and the other has 1 disc already (so row 2 is Yellow's — 1 empty cell below it). Mark the row-2 cell in the empty column with 'tg' (Red's) and the row-2 cell in the 1-disc column with 'td' (Yellow's). Keep other columns neutral. Legend: 'tg' = Row 2 here belongs to Red, 'td' = Row 2 here belongs to Yellow.</board instructions>

This is the critical trap: the same row number belongs to different players in different columns, depending on how many discs are already there. Row 2 in a fresh column belongs to Red (it is the 3rd disc, Red's turn). Row 2 in a column that already has one disc belongs to Yellow (it is the 2nd disc to be placed, Yellow's turn).

The shortcut: **subtract the current column height from the row number.** If the result is even, Red owns it; if odd, Yellow owns it.

coachMessages.text: A threat is only real if the right player lands on the completing cell. Who will get there first in this column?

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show a mid-game position where Red has three discs forming a horizontal line whose completing cell is at row 2 in a column of current height 0. Also show a second identical-looking setup (same row number) but in a column of current height 1, where Yellow would reach that cell first instead. Mark the valid Red threat cell (column height 0, row 2 → Red's) with 'tg' and the invalid one (column height 1, row 2 → Yellow's) with 'td'. Legend: 'tg' = Red's real threat (Red lands here), 'td' = Ghost threat (Yellow lands here first).</board instructions>

A threat is only as good as who lands on the completing cell. Before trusting any threat, ask: will I actually reach that cell, or will my opponent get there first? This is the question that Claimeven, Z-Threats, and all parity-based strategies are built on — and it all comes back to this one rule: count from the current column height.

socratic.goalPrompt: Two columns each have an empty cell at row 2. In which column does Red naturally land on row 2 as the columns fill up?
socratic._boardInstructions: Show a mid-game board with two candidate columns: Column A has 0 discs (empty), Column B has 1 disc (Red at row 0). Both have an empty cell at row 2. The student must identify Column A (height 0, row 2 → even gap of 2 → Red lands there) as the column where Red owns row 2. Mark the two candidate cells but leave the student to reason about which belongs to Red.
